papers.title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Kai Lu, Chenyang Ma, Ioannis Havoutis
papers.what: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (
papers.summary: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx

papers.title: ScaleWorld: High-Resolution World Generation through Shared Prediction and Refinement
papers.authors: Yansong Qu, Wesker Zheng, Quanjian Song, Zhiyuan Zhang et al.
papers.what: High-resolution generation enables video world models to render fine-grained scene structures and textures, but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. We present ScaleWorld, a causal video model that unifies low-resolution world prediction and hi
papers.summary: High-resolution generation enables video world models to render fine-grained scene structures and textures, but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. We present ScaleWorld, a causal video model that unifies low-resolution world prediction and high-resolution refinement within a single shared backbone. By refining its own predictions, ScaleWorld produces high-resolution world videos without requiring a separate refinement model. For each video chunk, the shared backbone first completes a low-resolution prediction and then performs one-step high-resolution refinement conditioned on that prediction. To support efficient streaming generation, we maintain separate causal states with a long low-resolution history for prediction and a short high-resolution history for refinement. To address task interference during distillation, we separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation and introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD). This procedure transfers prediction and refinement behaviors from specialized teachers into a shared student through local velocity matching under their respective sampling and history policies. {Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScaleWorld achieves high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.

papers.title: Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher
papers.authors: Yang Meng, Zixin Ding, Robert L. Grossman, Yuxin Chen
papers.what: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train thi
papers.summary: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor's error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a policy restricted to what is visible at deployment.

papers.title: Deterministic Temporal Embedding for Calcium Imaging Trace Extraction
papers.authors: Qi Gao, Julius Beichert, Miriam Ratliff, Karl Rohr
papers.what: Reliable extraction of calcium-dependent fluorescence traces in calcium imaging sequences requires identifying pixels whose fluorescence intensity reflects the same underlying cellular activity. We present a deterministic temporal embedding framework that maps pixel-wise fluorescence traces to a low
papers.summary: Reliable extraction of calcium-dependent fluorescence traces in calcium imaging sequences requires identifying pixels whose fluorescence intensity reflects the same underlying cellular activity. We present a deterministic temporal embedding framework that maps pixel-wise fluorescence traces to a low-dimensional representation in which temporally coherent sources form spatially coherent regions. Starting from a fuzzy-neighborhood graph and spectral initialization, we optimize a class-balanced cross-entropy objective using exact sparse attraction and a deterministic particle-mesh decomposition of the dense repulsive interaction with sparse edge compensation, avoiding stochastic negative sampling. The resulting latent representation is spatially decoded into reliable source supports for trace extraction without imposing an explicit cellular shape prior. Experiments on synthetic and in vivo two-photon calcium imaging data demonstrate robust recovery of irregular and spatially touching sources together with efficient deterministic embedding optimization.

papers.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
papers.authors: Mengxiao Wang, Mahbub Alam, Kalyan Nakka, Nitesh Saxena
papers.what: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)valid
papers.summary: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

papers.title: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video
papers.authors: Yiyan Ji, Qixun Wang, Yang Shi, Zhuoran Zhang et al.
papers.what: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled
papers.summary: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.

papers.title: MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models
papers.authors: Jinzhe Li, Qi Wang, Dandan Guo, Li Liu et al.
papers.what: When multimodal decision models determine actions, moderation outcomes, or quality judgments, their reliability depends on preserving semantic decisions across presentation changes, ignoring irrelevant additions, and distinguishing information consistent with task evidence from information that conf
papers.summary: When multimodal decision models determine actions, moderation outcomes, or quality judgments, their reliability depends on preserving semantic decisions across presentation changes, ignoring irrelevant additions, and distinguishing information consistent with task evidence from information that conflicts with it. Existing evaluations study decision-interface biases and multimodal model behavior in separate settings, leaving no common protocol to compare multimodal decision models with their backbones on practical tasks. We introduce \textbf{MM-SystemOneBias}, which evaluates 13 models on 5,323 original instances from nine public datasets and 11 task scenarios using six paired interventions: option order, option label, external judgment, image--text description, irrelevant information, and rating scale. Across seven matched decision-model--backbone pairs, decision models are more stable under option-label, irrelevant-information, and rating-scale changes in all seven pairs; six pairs also show lower option-order flip rates. They incur smaller accuracy losses under incorrect external judgments in all seven pairs and conflicting descriptions in six. In six pairs, they gain less accuracy from correct external judgments and show less favorable accuracy changes under consistent descriptions. Among pairs with unchanged semantic decisions, mean absolute changes in answer probabilities range from 4.56 to 11.55 percentage points, revealing input effects that accuracy alone misses.

papers.title: WizardLM: Empowering large pre-trained language models to follow complex instructions
papers.authors: Can Xu, Qing‐Feng Sun, Zheng, Kai, Xiubo Geng et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Training large language models (LLMs) with open-domain instruction following data brings colossal success. However, manually creating such instruction data is very time-consuming and labor-intensive. Moreover, humans may struggle to produce high-complexity instructions. In this p
papers.summary: Training large language models (LLMs) with open-domain instruction following data brings colossal success. However, manually creating such instruction data is very time-consuming and labor-intensive. Moreover, humans may struggle to produce high-complexity instructions. In this paper, we show an avenue for creating large amounts of instruction data with varying levels of complexity using LLM instead of humans. Starting with an initial set of instructions, we use our proposed Evol-Instruct to rewrite them step by step into more complex instructions. Then, we mix all generated instruction data to fine-tune LLaMA. We call the resulting model WizardLM. Human evaluations on a complexity-balanced test bed and Vicuna's testset show that instructions from Evol-Instruct are superior to human-created ones. By analyzing the human evaluation results of the high complexity part, we demonstrate that outputs from our WizardLM are preferred to outputs from OpenAI ChatGPT. In GPT-4 automatic evaluation, WizardLM achieves more than 90\% capacity of ChatGPT on 17 out of 29 skills. Even though WizardLM still lags behind ChatGPT in some aspects, our findings suggest that fine-tuning with AI-evolved instructions is a promising direction for enhancing LLMs. Our code and data are public at https://github.com/nlpxucan/WizardLM

papers.title: ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs
papers.authors: Qin, Yujia, Shihao Liang, Yining Ye, Kunlun Zhu et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Despite the advancements of open-source large language models (LLMs), e.g., LLaMA, they remain significantly limited in tool-use capabilities, i.e., using external tools (APIs) to fulfill human instructions. The reason is that current instruction tuning largely focuses on basic l
papers.summary: Despite the advancements of open-source large language models (LLMs), e.g., LLaMA, they remain significantly limited in tool-use capabilities, i.e., using external tools (APIs) to fulfill human instructions. The reason is that current instruction tuning largely focuses on basic language tasks but ignores the tool-use domain. This is in contrast to the excellent tool-use capabilities of state-of-the-art (SOTA) closed-source LLMs, e.g., ChatGPT. To bridge this gap, we introduce ToolLLM, a general tool-use framework encompassing data construction, model training, and evaluation. We first present ToolBench, an instruction-tuning dataset for tool use, which is constructed automatically using ChatGPT. Specifically, the construction can be divided into three stages: (i) API collection: we collect 16,464 real-world RESTful APIs spanning 49 categories from RapidAPI Hub; (ii) instruction generation: we prompt ChatGPT to generate diverse instructions involving these APIs, covering both single-tool and multi-tool scenarios; (iii) solution path annotation: we use ChatGPT to search for a valid solution path (chain of API calls) for each instruction. To enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, we develop a novel depth-first search-based decision tree algorithm. It enables LLMs to evaluate multiple reasoning traces and expand the search space. Moreover, to evaluate the tool-use capabilities of LLMs, we develop an automatic evaluator: ToolEval. Based on ToolBench, we fine-tune LLaMA to obtain an LLM ToolLLaMA, and equip it with a neural API retriever to recommend appropriate APIs for each instruction. Experiments show that ToolLLaMA demonstrates a remarkable ability to execute complex instructions and generalize to unseen APIs, and exhibits comparable performance to ChatGPT. Our ToolLLaMA also demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization ability in an out-of-distribution tool-use dataset: APIBench.

papers.title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
papers.authors: Tri Dao
papers.what: [Conference] Scaling Transformers to longer sequence lengths has been a major problem in the last several years, promising to improve performance in language modeling and high-resolution image understanding, as well as to unlock new applications in code, audio, and video generation. The atten
papers.summary: Scaling Transformers to longer sequence lengths has been a major problem in the last several years, promising to improve performance in language modeling and high-resolution image understanding, as well as to unlock new applications in code, audio, and video generation. The attention layer is the main bottleneck in scaling to longer sequences, as its runtime and memory increase quadratically in the sequence length. FlashAttention exploits the asymmetric GPU memory hierarchy to bring significant memory saving (linear instead of quadratic) and runtime speedup (2-4$\times$ compared to optimized baselines), with no approximation. However, FlashAttention is still not nearly as fast as optimized matrix-multiply (GEMM) operations, reaching only 25-40\% of the theoretical maximum FLOPs/s. We observe that the inefficiency is due to suboptimal work partitioning between different thread blocks and warps on the GPU, causing either low-occupancy or unnecessary shared memory reads/writes. We propose FlashAttention-2, with better work partitioning to address these issues. In particular, we (1) tweak the algorithm to reduce the number of non-matmul FLOPs (2) parallelize the attention computation, even for a single head, across different thread blocks to increase occupancy, and (3) within each thread block, distribute the work between warps to reduce communication through shared memory. These yield around 2$\times$ speedup compared to FlashAttention, reaching 50-73\% of the theoretical maximum FLOPs/s on A100 and getting close to the efficiency of GEMM operations. We empirically validate that when used end-to-end to train GPT-style models, FlashAttention-2 reaches training speed of up to 225 TFLOPs/s per A100 GPU (72\% model FLOPs utilization).

papers.title: Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
papers.authors: Xinyun Chen, Maxwell Lin, Nathanael Schärli, Denny Zhou
papers.what: [Conference] Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive performance on code generation. However, for complex programming tasks, generating the correct solution in one go becomes challenging, thus some prior works have designed program repair approaches to improve code generation pe
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive performance on code generation. However, for complex programming tasks, generating the correct solution in one go becomes challenging, thus some prior works have designed program repair approaches to improve code generation performance. In this work, we propose Self-Debugging, which teaches a large language model to debug its predicted program via few-shot demonstrations. In particular, we demonstrate that Self-Debugging can teach the large language model to perform rubber duck debugging; i.e., without any human feedback on the code correctness or error messages, the model is able to identify its mistakes by investigating the execution results and explaining the generated code in natural language. Self-Debugging achieves the state-of-the-art performance on several code generation benchmarks, including the Spider dataset for text-to-SQL generation, TransCoder for C++-to-Python translation, and MBPP for text-to-Python generation. On the Spider benchmark where there are no unit tests to verify the correctness of predictions, Self-Debugging with code explanation consistently improves the baseline by 2-3%, and improves the prediction accuracy on problems of the hardest level by 9%. On TransCoder and MBPP where unit tests are available, Self-Debugging improves the baseline accuracy by up to 12%. Meanwhile, by leveraging feedback messages and reusing failed predictions, Self-Debugging notably improves sample efficiency, and can match or outperform baseline models that generate more than 10x candidate programs.

papers.title: Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!
papers.authors: Xiangyu Qi, Yi Zeng, Tinghao Xie, Pin‐Yu Chen et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Optimizing large language models (LLMs) for downstream use cases often involves the customization of pre-trained LLMs through further fine-tuning. Meta's open release of Llama models and OpenAI's APIs for fine-tuning GPT-3.5 Turbo on custom datasets also encourage this practice.
papers.summary: Optimizing large language models (LLMs) for downstream use cases often involves the customization of pre-trained LLMs through further fine-tuning. Meta's open release of Llama models and OpenAI's APIs for fine-tuning GPT-3.5 Turbo on custom datasets also encourage this practice. But, what are the safety costs associated with such custom fine-tuning? We note that while existing safety alignment infrastructures can restrict harmful behaviors of LLMs at inference time, they do not cover safety risks when fine-tuning privileges are extended to end-users. Our red teaming studies find that the safety alignment of LLMs can be compromised by fine-tuning with only a few adversarially designed training examples. For instance, we jailbreak GPT-3.5 Turbo's safety guardrails by fine-tuning it on only 10 such examples at a cost of less than $0.20 via OpenAI's APIs, making the model responsive to nearly any harmful instructions. Disconcertingly, our research also reveals that, even without malicious intent, simply fine-tuning with benign and commonly used datasets can also inadvertently degrade the safety alignment of LLMs, though to a lesser extent. These findings suggest that fine-tuning aligned LLMs introduces new safety risks that current safety infrastructures fall short of addressing -- even if a model's initial safety alignment is impeccable, it is not necessarily to be maintained after custom fine-tuning. We outline and critically analyze potential mitigations and advocate for further research efforts toward reinforcing safety protocols for the custom fine-tuning of aligned LLMs.

papers.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
papers.authors: Xiao Liu, Hao Yu, Hanchen Zhang, Yifan Xu et al.
papers.what: [Conference] The potential of Large Language Model (LLM) as agents has been widely acknowledged recently. Thus, there is an urgent need to quantitatively \textit{evaluate LLMs as agents} on challenging tasks in interactive environments. We present AgentBench, a multi-dimensional benchmark tha
papers.summary: The potential of Large Language Model (LLM) as agents has been widely acknowledged recently. Thus, there is an urgent need to quantitatively \textit{evaluate LLMs as agents} on challenging tasks in interactive environments. We present AgentBench, a multi-dimensional benchmark that consists of 8 distinct environments to assess LLM-as-Agent's reasoning and decision-making abilities. Our extensive test over \num API-based and open-sourced (OSS) LLMs shows that, while top commercial LLMs present a strong ability of acting as agents in complex environments, there is a significant disparity in performance between them and many OSS competitors that are no larger than 70B. We identify the typical reasons of failures in environments and LLMs, showing that poor long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction following abilities are the main obstacles for developing usable LLM agents. Improving instruction following and training on high quality multi-round alignment data could improve agent performance. And different from existing assumptions, training on code present ambivalent impacts on different agent tasks. Datasets, environments, and an integrated evaluation package for AgentBench are released at https://github.com/THUDM/AgentBench.

papers.title: ChatEval: Towards Better LLM-based Evaluators through Multi-Agent Debate
papers.authors: Chi-Min Chan, Weize Chen, Yusheng Su, Jianxuan Yu et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Text evaluation has historically posed significant challenges, often demanding substantial labor and time cost. With the emergence of large language models (LLMs), researchers have explored LLMs' potential as alternatives for human evaluation. While these single-agent-based appro
papers.summary: Text evaluation has historically posed significant challenges, often demanding substantial labor and time cost. With the emergence of large language models (LLMs), researchers have explored LLMs' potential as alternatives for human evaluation. While these single-agent-based approaches show promise, experimental results suggest that further advancements are needed to bridge the gap between their current effectiveness and human-level evaluation quality. Recognizing that best practices of human evaluation processes often involve multiple human annotators collaborating in the evaluation, we resort to a multi-agent debate framework, moving beyond single-agent prompting strategies. The multi-agent-based approach enables a group of LLMs to synergize with an array of intelligent counterparts, harnessing their distinct capabilities and expertise to enhance efficiency and effectiveness in handling intricate tasks. In this paper, we construct a multi-agent referee team called ChatEval to autonomously discuss and evaluate the quality of generated responses from different models on open-ended questions and traditional natural language generation (NLG) tasks. Our analysis shows that ChatEval transcends mere textual scoring, offering a human-mimicking evaluation process for reliable assessments. Our code is available at https://github.com/chanchimin/ChatEval.

papers.title: Training Diffusion Models with Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Kevin Black, Janner, Michael, Yilun Du, Ilya Kostrikov et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Diffusion models are a class of flexible generative models trained with an approximation to the log-likelihood objective. However, most use cases of diffusion models are not concerned with likelihoods, but instead with downstream objectives such as human-perceived image quality o
papers.summary: Diffusion models are a class of flexible generative models trained with an approximation to the log-likelihood objective. However, most use cases of diffusion models are not concerned with likelihoods, but instead with downstream objectives such as human-perceived image quality or drug effectiveness. In this paper, we investigate reinforcement learning methods for directly optimizing diffusion models for such objectives. We describe how posing denoising as a multi-step decision-making problem enables a class of policy gradient algorithms, which we refer to as denoising diffusion policy optimization (DDPO), that are more effective than alternative reward-weighted likelihood approaches. Empirically, DDPO is able to adapt text-to-image diffusion models to objectives that are difficult to express via prompting, such as image compressibility, and those derived from human feedback, such as aesthetic quality. Finally, we show that DDPO can improve prompt-image alignment using feedback from a vision-language model without the need for additional data collection or human annotation. The project's website can be found at http://rl-diffusion.github.io .

papers.title: YaRN: Efficient Context Window Extension of Large Language Models
papers.authors: Peng, Bowen, Jeffrey Quesnelle, Honglu Fan, Enrico Shippole
papers.what: [Conference] Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) have been shown to effectively encode positional information in transformer-based language models. However, these models fail to generalize past the sequence length they were trained on. We present YaRN (Yet another RoPE extensioN method), a comp
papers.summary: Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) have been shown to effectively encode positional information in transformer-based language models. However, these models fail to generalize past the sequence length they were trained on. We present YaRN (Yet another RoPE extensioN method), a compute-efficient method to extend the context window of such models, requiring 10x less tokens and 2.5x less training steps than previous methods. Using YaRN, we show that LLaMA models can effectively utilize and extrapolate to context lengths much longer than their original pre-training would allow, while also surpassing previous the state-of-the-art at context window extension. In addition, we demonstrate that YaRN exhibits the capability to extrapolate beyond the limited context of a fine-tuning dataset. Code is available at https://github.com/jquesnelle/yarn

papers.title: $τ$-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
papers.authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
papers.what: [Conference] Existing benchmarks do not test language agents on their interaction with human users or ability to follow domain-specific rules, both of which are vital for deploying them in real world applications. We propose $τ$-bench, a benchmark emulating dynamic conversations between a use
papers.summary: Existing benchmarks do not test language agents on their interaction with human users or ability to follow domain-specific rules, both of which are vital for deploying them in real world applications. We propose $τ$-bench, a benchmark emulating dynamic conversations between a user (simulated by language models) and a language agent provided with domain-specific API tools and policy guidelines. We employ an efficient and faithful evaluation process that compares the database state at the end of a conversation with the annotated goal state. We also propose a new metric (pass^k) to evaluate the reliability of agent behavior over multiple trials. Our experiments show that even state-of-the-art function calling agents (like gpt-4o) succeed on <50% of the tasks, and are quite inconsistent (pass^8 <25% in retail). Our findings point to the need for methods that can improve the ability of agents to act consistently and follow rules reliably.

papers.title: LongVideoBench: A Benchmark for Long-context Interleaved Video-Language Understanding
papers.authors: Haoning Wu, Dongxu Li, Bei Chen, Junnan Li
papers.what: [Conference] Large multimodal models (LMMs) are processing increasingly longer and richer inputs. Albeit the progress, few public benchmark is available to measure such development. To mitigate this gap, we introduce LongVideoBench, a question-answering benchmark that features video-language
papers.summary: Large multimodal models (LMMs) are processing increasingly longer and richer inputs. Albeit the progress, few public benchmark is available to measure such development. To mitigate this gap, we introduce LongVideoBench, a question-answering benchmark that features video-language interleaved inputs up to an hour long. Our benchmark includes 3,763 varying-length web-collected videos with their subtitles across diverse themes, designed to comprehensively evaluate LMMs on long-term multimodal understanding. To achieve this, we interpret the primary challenge as to accurately retrieve and reason over detailed multimodal information from long inputs. As such, we formulate a novel video question-answering task termed referring reasoning. Specifically, as part of the question, it contains a referring query that references related video contexts, called referred context. The model is then required to reason over relevant video details from the referred context. Following the paradigm of referring reasoning, we curate 6,678 human-annotated multiple-choice questions in 17 fine-grained categories, establishing one of the most comprehensive benchmarks for long-form video understanding. Evaluations suggest that the LongVideoBench presents significant challenges even for the most advanced proprietary models (e.g. GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro, GPT-4-Turbo), while their open-source counterparts show an even larger performance gap. In addition, our results indicate that model performance on the benchmark improves only when they are capable of processing more frames, positioning LongVideoBench as a valuable benchmark for evaluating future-generation long-context LMMs.

papers.title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
papers.authors: Omar Khattab, Arnav Singhvi, Paridhi Maheshwari, Zhiyuan Zhang et al.
papers.what: [Conference] The ML community is rapidly exploring techniques for prompting language models (LMs) and for stacking them into pipelines that solve complex tasks. Unfortunately, existing LM pipelines are typically implemented using hard-coded "prompt templates", i.e. lengthy strings discovered
papers.summary: The ML community is rapidly exploring techniques for prompting language models (LMs) and for stacking them into pipelines that solve complex tasks. Unfortunately, existing LM pipelines are typically implemented using hard-coded "prompt templates", i.e. lengthy strings discovered via trial and error. Toward a more systematic approach for developing and optimizing LM pipelines, we introduce DSPy, a programming model that abstracts LM pipelines as text transformation graphs, i.e. imperative computational graphs where LMs are invoked through declarative modules. DSPy modules are parameterized, meaning they can learn (by creating and collecting demonstrations) how to apply compositions of prompting, finetuning, augmentation, and reasoning techniques. We design a compiler that will optimize any DSPy pipeline to maximize a given metric. We conduct two case studies, showing that succinct DSPy programs can express and optimize sophisticated LM pipelines that reason about math word problems, tackle multi-hop retrieval, answer complex questions, and control agent loops. Within minutes of compiling, a few lines of DSPy allow GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat to self-bootstrap pipelines that outperform standard few-shot prompting (generally by over 25% and 65%, respectively) and pipelines with expert-created demonstrations (by up to 5-46% and 16-40%, respectively). On top of that, DSPy programs compiled to open and relatively small LMs like 770M-parameter T5 and llama2-13b-chat are competitive with approaches that rely on expert-written prompt chains for proprietary GPT-3.5. DSPy is available at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy

papers.title: Depth Anything 3: Recovering the Visual Space from Any Views
papers.authors: Lin, Haotong, Chen, Sili, Liew, Junhao, Chen, Donny Y. et al.
papers.what: [Conference] We present Depth Anything 3 (DA3), a model that predicts spatially consistent geometry from an arbitrary number of visual inputs, with or without known camera poses. In pursuit of minimal modeling, DA3 yields two key insights: a single plain transformer (e.g., vanilla DINO encode
papers.summary: We present Depth Anything 3 (DA3), a model that predicts spatially consistent geometry from an arbitrary number of visual inputs, with or without known camera poses. In pursuit of minimal modeling, DA3 yields two key insights: a single plain transformer (e.g., vanilla DINO encoder) is sufficient as a backbone without architectural specialization, and a singular depth-ray prediction target obviates the need for complex multi-task learning. Through our teacher-student training paradigm, the model achieves a level of detail and generalization on par with Depth Anything 2 (DA2). We establish a new visual geometry benchmark covering camera pose estimation, any-view geometry and visual rendering. On this benchmark, DA3 sets a new state-of-the-art across all tasks, surpassing prior SOTA VGGT by an average of 44.3% in camera pose accuracy and 25.1% in geometric accuracy. Moreover, it outperforms DA2 in monocular depth estimation. All models are trained exclusively on public academic datasets.

papers.title: Diffusion Forcing: Next-token Prediction Meets Full-Sequence Diffusion
papers.authors: Boyuan Chen, Diego Martí Monsó, Yilun Du, Max Simchowitz et al.
papers.what: [Conference] This paper presents Diffusion Forcing, a new training paradigm where a diffusion model is trained to denoise a set of tokens with independent per-token noise levels. We apply Diffusion Forcing to sequence generative modeling by training a causal next-token prediction model to gen
papers.summary: This paper presents Diffusion Forcing, a new training paradigm where a diffusion model is trained to denoise a set of tokens with independent per-token noise levels. We apply Diffusion Forcing to sequence generative modeling by training a causal next-token prediction model to generate one or several future tokens without fully diffusing past ones. Our approach is shown to combine the strengths of next-token prediction models, such as variable-length generation, with the strengths of full-sequence diffusion models, such as the ability to guide sampling to desirable trajectories. Our method offers a range of additional capabilities, such as (1) rolling-out sequences of continuous tokens, such as video, with lengths past the training horizon, where baselines diverge and (2) new sampling and guiding schemes that uniquely profit from Diffusion Forcing's variable-horizon and causal architecture, and which lead to marked performance gains in decision-making and planning tasks. In addition to its empirical success, our method is proven to optimize a variational lower bound on the likelihoods of all subsequences of tokens drawn from the true joint distribution. Project website: https://boyuan.space/diffusion-forcing

papers.title: AgentVerse: Facilitating Multi-Agent Collaboration and Exploring Emergent Behaviors
papers.authors: Chen, Weize, Su, Yusheng, Jingwei Zuo, Cheng I. Yang et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Autonomous agents empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have undergone significant improvements, enabling them to generalize across a broad spectrum of tasks. However, in real-world scenarios, cooperation among individuals is often required to enhance the efficiency and effec
papers.summary: Autonomous agents empowered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have undergone significant improvements, enabling them to generalize across a broad spectrum of tasks. However, in real-world scenarios, cooperation among individuals is often required to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of task accomplishment. Hence, inspired by human group dynamics, we propose a multi-agent framework \framework that can collaboratively and dynamically adjust its composition as a greater-than-the-sum-of-its-parts system. Our experiments demonstrate that \framework framework can effectively deploy multi-agent groups that outperform a single agent. Furthermore, we delve into the emergence of social behaviors among individual agents within a group during collaborative task accomplishment. In view of these behaviors, we discuss some possible strategies to leverage positive ones and mitigate negative ones for improving the collaborative potential of multi-agent groups. Our codes for \framework will soon be released at \url{https://github.com/OpenBMB/AgentVerse}.

papers.title: CogVideoX: Text-to-Video Diffusion Models with An Expert Transformer
papers.authors: Zhuoyi Yang, Jiayan Teng, Wendi Zheng, Ding, Ming et al.
papers.what: [Conference] We present CogVideoX, a large-scale text-to-video generation model based on diffusion transformer, which can generate 10-second continuous videos aligned with text prompt, with a frame rate of 16 fps and resolution of 768 * 1360 pixels. Previous video generation models often had
papers.summary: We present CogVideoX, a large-scale text-to-video generation model based on diffusion transformer, which can generate 10-second continuous videos aligned with text prompt, with a frame rate of 16 fps and resolution of 768 * 1360 pixels. Previous video generation models often had limited movement and short durations, and is difficult to generate videos with coherent narratives based on text. We propose several designs to address these issues. First, we propose a 3D Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to compress videos along both spatial and temporal dimensions, to improve both compression rate and video fidelity. Second, to improve the text-video alignment, we propose an expert transformer with the expert adaptive LayerNorm to facilitate the deep fusion between the two modalities. Third, by employing a progressive training and multi-resolution frame pack technique, CogVideoX is adept at producing coherent, long-duration, different shape videos characterized by significant motions. In addition, we develop an effective text-video data processing pipeline that includes various data preprocessing strategies and a video captioning method, greatly contributing to the generation quality and semantic alignment. Results show that CogVideoX demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across both multiple machine metrics and human evaluations. The model weight of both 3D Causal VAE, Video caption model and CogVideoX are publicly available at https://github.com/THUDM/CogVideo.

papers.title: Gaussian Splatting SLAM
papers.authors: Hidenobu Matsuki, Riku Murai, Paul H. J. Kelly, Andrew J. Davison
papers.what: [Conference] We present the first application of 3D Gaussian Splatting in monocular SLAM, the most fundamental but the hardest setup for Visual SLAM. Our method, which runs live at 3fps, utilises Gaussians as the only 3D representation, unifying the required representation for accurate, effic
papers.summary: We present the first application of 3D Gaussian Splatting in monocular SLAM, the most fundamental but the hardest setup for Visual SLAM. Our method, which runs live at 3fps, utilises Gaussians as the only 3D representation, unifying the required representation for accurate, efficient tracking, mapping, and high-quality rendering. Designed for challenging monocular settings, our approach is seamlessly extendable to RGB-D SLAM when an external depth sensor is available. Several innovations are required to continuously reconstruct 3D scenes with high fidelity from a live camera. First, to move beyond the original 3DGS algorithm, which requires accurate poses from an offline Structure from Motion (SfM) system, we formulate camera tracking for 3DGS using direct optimisation against the 3D Gaussians, and show that this enables fast and robust tracking with a wide basin of convergence. Second, by utilising the explicit nature of the Gaussians, we introduce geometric verification and regularisation to handle the ambiguities occurring in incremental 3D dense reconstruction. Finally, we introduce afull SLAM system which not only achieves state-of-the-art results in novel view synthesis and trajectory estimation but also reconstruction of tiny and even transparent objects.

papers.title: DreamGaussian: Generative Gaussian Splatting for Efficient 3D Content Creation
papers.authors: Jiaxiang Tang, Jiawei Ren, Hang Zhou, Ziwei Liu et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Recent advances in 3D content creation mostly leverage optimization-based 3D generation via score distillation sampling (SDS). Though promising results have been exhibited, these methods often suffer from slow per-sample optimization, limiting their practical usage. In this paper
papers.summary: Recent advances in 3D content creation mostly leverage optimization-based 3D generation via score distillation sampling (SDS). Though promising results have been exhibited, these methods often suffer from slow per-sample optimization, limiting their practical usage. In this paper, we propose DreamGaussian, a novel 3D content generation framework that achieves both efficiency and quality simultaneously. Our key insight is to design a generative 3D Gaussian Splatting model with companioned mesh extraction and texture refinement in UV space. In contrast to the occupancy pruning used in Neural Radiance Fields, we demonstrate that the progressive densification of 3D Gaussians converges significantly faster for 3D generative tasks. To further enhance the texture quality and facilitate downstream applications, we introduce an efficient algorithm to convert 3D Gaussians into textured meshes and apply a fine-tuning stage to refine the details. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior efficiency and competitive generation quality of our proposed approach. Notably, DreamGaussian produces high-quality textured meshes in just 2 minutes from a single-view image, achieving approximately 10 times acceleration compared to existing methods.

papers.title: Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
papers.authors: Haocheng Mei, Yuchuan Tian, Yingte Shu, Chao Xu et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a gr
papers.summary: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a graded audit. We test attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes, and survey C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 commercial endpoints. Only authenticated provenance supports accusations: tier contradictions or duplicate signed instances under fresh-generation contracts, excluding retries and idempotent returns. Unverifiable signed-endpoint deliveries trigger original-file demands under pass-through clauses; archive-reuse and delivery-parameter screens support review only. Six-model container and bitstream accuracy falls from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, using different feature sets. Subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988. Only BytePlus authenticates tier claims under our pinned policy, including 187/187 audited deliveries across three Seedance tiers; tested remuxing and re-encoding leave processed Seedance files unverifiable. The audit identifies authenticated contradictions in 100/100 raw 720p signed tier-swap cases, with zero observed false flags on the tested honest pools.

papers.title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
papers.authors: Shibo Zhou, Tianqi Hong, Zheng Yan, He Yang
papers.what: [Explore] Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specif
papers.summary: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.

papers.title: The Statistical Cost of Second-Order Orthogonality
papers.authors: Juan Carlos Escanciano, Joël R. Terschuur
papers.what: [Explore] Debiased machine learning removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation, but the remaining quadratic bias can invalidate inference when nuisance functions are hard to learn. Second-order orthogonal moments remove this bias at the cost of additional variance. We characteri
papers.summary: Debiased machine learning removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation, but the remaining quadratic bias can invalidate inference when nuisance functions are hard to learn. Second-order orthogonal moments remove this bias at the cost of additional variance. We characterize this cost as the minimum variance of a correction that offsets the quadratic sensitivity of the moment to nuisance errors, and show that exact correction is possible only when this cost is finite. Because the cost varies across moments, the first-order efficient moment need not minimize total variance. We therefore choose the moment and its correction jointly, and derive the resulting minimum variance, a second-order analogue of the semiparametric efficiency bound. The optimal moment may trade first-order efficiency for a lower correction cost. In a binary choice logit model, it uses information beyond the conditional likelihood only in well-populated covariate cells; in difference-in-differences with continuous covariates, exact correction forgoes the efficiency gains from exclusion restrictions. In the partially linear model with continuous controls, the cost is infinite for every moment, so that only part of the bias can be removed. For such cases, we propose a data-driven adaptive rule that chooses how much bias to remove within a bound on variance inflation, and we show that inference remains valid after selection. In simulations for the partially linear model, the coverage of nominal 95\% intervals rises from 32--80\% to 94--97\% in all designs but a stress test.

papers.title: GenSPARQL: A Generative Extension of SPARQL for Incomplete Knowledge Graphs
papers.authors: Jingcheng Wu, Yi Wang, Hongkuan Zhou, Steffen Staab et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Knowledge graphs on the Web are incomplete, and SPARQL answers a query only from the stored triples. Large language models (LLMs) can predict missing facts, but an LLM returns names instead of IRIs and requires one call per binding of a query variable. We present GenSPARQL, a gen
papers.summary: Knowledge graphs on the Web are incomplete, and SPARQL answers a query only from the stored triples. Large language models (LLMs) can predict missing facts, but an LLM returns names instead of IRIs and requires one call per binding of a query variable. We present GenSPARQL, a generative extension of SPARQL 1.1 with an operator GENOP that binds values generated by an LLM to query variables during query evaluation. A similarity join maps generated names to entities of the graph, and the query planner invokes the LLM only for the bindings selected by the other graph patterns and filters. In a web workbench, attendees query two graphs built from Wikidata and inspect generated values, mapped entities and LLM calls. In our evaluation with three open-weight LLMs, the embedding similarity maps 83% of the entities named by the LLMs and yields only one incorrect match.

papers.title: Ground Truth Bias in AI-Assisted Medical Annotation: A Crossover Study Using an Independent Radiologist Reference Standard
papers.authors: Márton Baltay, Tamás Ilcsik, Márton Borbély
papers.what: [Explore] Behavioural evaluations of artificial-intelligence-assisted annotation score every human decision against a reference standard, so their conclusions inherit that standard's validity. We tested how far conclusions about assistance, reliance and individual differences depend on it.
papers.summary: Behavioural evaluations of artificial-intelligence-assisted annotation score every human decision against a reference standard, so their conclusions inherit that standard's validity. We tested how far conclusions about assistance, reliance and individual differences depend on it. Fifty-one non-expert high-school students annotated 50 knee radiographs for osteoarthritis, with and without a deliberately imperfect classifier, in a crossover design; personality and non-verbal reasoning were also measured. Decisions were scored against the public repository labels and against an independent reference standard from a radiologist panel, which graded 23 of the 50 images as indeterminate. Against the repository labels, assistance raised accuracy from 60.4% to 65.3% (odds ratio 1.23, p=0.002). Against the independent standard, the gain on the 27 determinate images was smaller and not significant in the primary model (78.4% to 80.8%; odds ratio 1.16, p=0.178). The apparent benefit had been concentrated on the indeterminate images and was not significant when those images were assigned to either class. The direction of residual over-reliance depended on how indeterminate cases were handled, and the personality trait most strongly associated with accuracy changed identity and sign between standards. Reliance measures are only as valid as the reference standard that defines when the assistant is right.

papers.title: Structural Fine-Tuning under Economic Restrictions
papers.authors: Yi Niu, Yuecheng Su, Ethan Yang
papers.what: [Explore] How should a predictor trained on historical data be adapted to a new economic environment or task when few target observations are available? We propose structural fine-tuning, a framework that introduces economic restrictions to guide the adaptation of pretrained predictors. Th
papers.summary: How should a predictor trained on historical data be adapted to a new economic environment or task when few target observations are available? We propose structural fine-tuning, a framework that introduces economic restrictions to guide the adaptation of pretrained predictors. The framework does not require a complete structural model; instead, it utilizes constraints based on economic knowledge, ranging from simple, ubiquitous assumptions to particular workhorse models. Theoretically, we characterize conditions when economic restrictions improve prediction over the original model and ordinary fine-tuning. Then, we illustrate the framework through a simulation exercise of a credit issuer's credit-limit decision following a Medicaid-style expansion in medical payments. Imposing restrictions based on eligibility, outstanding medical bills, cash flows, and group-level risk bounds, our framework lowers the root mean squared error of predicted risk by 28 to 39 percent and the issuer's policy regret by 3 to 10 percent relative to ordinary neuron gating, LoRA, and full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Presenting Your Figures: Data-informed Animated Transitions Across Scientific Figure Panels
papers.authors: Lu Ying, Can Liu, Yuxiao Yang, Jianing Yin et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Multi-panel figures are commonly used in research papers to show scientific data, and researchers often reuse them when presenting their work. Presenting these figures often involves explaining how data across chart panels are related. Animated transitions can progressively revea
papers.summary: Multi-panel figures are commonly used in research papers to show scientific data, and researchers often reuse them when presenting their work. Presenting these figures often involves explaining how data across chart panels are related. Animated transitions can progressively reveal these relationships, but two static panels specify only the endpoints, leaving what intermediate keyframes should show and how the transition should progress unclear. To support transition design across diverse scientific figures, we developed Figure Space and Transition Space through iterative analysis of 48 published multi-panel figures across eight scientific subject areas. Figure Space represents panel composition, data transformations, and visual encodings while retaining the links needed to trace panel results back to records. Transition Space uses this representation and source data to construct and sequence keyframes that make corresponding data visible and align them while preserving the meaning of each panel's position encodings. Building on these spaces, we developed FigFlux, a human-in-the-loop authoring system that guides AI agents in generating animated transitions from a multi-panel figure and its associated materials. Researchers can revise keyframes in natural language before animation generation. We evaluate FigFlux through cross-domain case studies, a study with 16 scientific authors, and expert assessment. Authors reported lower overall workload than with their familiar tools, while experts gave FigFlux transitions higher ratings than transitions created with participants' familiar tools or generated by AI alone. The example gallery have been published online: https://figflux.github.io.

papers.title: RouterWeave: A Unified Observation Layer for Cross-Platform Activity Analysis via Home Routers
papers.authors: Chengeng Liu, Ronghua Li, Yan Long, Shinan Liu
papers.what: [Explore] Smart homes bring together devices from different operating systems and vendor ecosystems, but each platform reports activity only for the devices and features it supports, leaving gaps in household-wide activity monitoring. Interoperability standards such as Matter and software
papers.summary: Smart homes bring together devices from different operating systems and vendor ecosystems, but each platform reports activity only for the devices and features it supports, leaving gaps in household-wide activity monitoring. Interoperability standards such as Matter and software integrations connect and control supported devices, yet vendor restrictions and licensing barriers limit access to their data, while hardware constraints hinder integration. Our key insight is that encrypted network traffic provides complementary evidence of activity across platform boundaries. Accordingly, we present RouterWeave, a router-side observation framework that combines cross-platform traffic collection, task-adaptive processing, and unified activity records. These records preserve activity meaning, temporal extent, and source-device attribution while distinguishing discrete operations from sustained activity intervals. We evaluate RouterWeave across four datasets, native execution on a commodity home router, and two novel case studies: cross-platform Screen Time monitoring and appliance energy estimation. RouterWeave achieves 94.41% macro-F1 on application activities and 97.46% on IoT operations, outperforming baselines by up to 20.99 percentage points, while using under 7 MB of router memory per task and supporting 54 concurrent devices within a 5-second update window. In end-to-end case studies, RouterWeave reconstructs 600 Screen Time timelines across Android, iOS, and Windows with 92.15% accuracy (24.84-second mean active-time error over 19-minute averages) and recovers 49 of 55 appliance operations over four days, tracking ON/OFF states with 92.84% agreement and estimating electricity use within a 4.28% error. Together, these results establish the commodity home router as practical infrastructure for whole-home activity sensing. The code is open sourced at https://github.com/naisslab/routerweave.

papers.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
papers.authors: Xuankun Rong, Xinhao Deng, Wenzhang Jiang, Ziheng Peng et al.
papers.what: [Explore] As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful reque
papers.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

papers.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
papers.authors: Yuzhi Huang, Jie Wu, Fanding Huang, Junchao Lin et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and ex
papers.summary: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

papers.title: ACE-Brain-0.7: Learning Execution-Grounded Reasoning for Embodied Agents
papers.authors: Yinhe Wang, Shijun Shi, Feng Pan, Tao Tao et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state. We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision--language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation. To train the model, we curate 3.7
papers.summary: Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state. We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision--language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation. To train the model, we curate 3.7 million question--answer pairs, drawing execution supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation. These questions span different stages of an execution and connect task-level judgments with observed progress and outcomes. We then fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this collection together with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data. Across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, ACE-Brain-0.7 achieves an average score of 76.5, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 72.7 and Claude Opus 5.5 at 73.5. Our model also leads the evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and reaching 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg. Controlled evaluations further indicate that our task-only model makes more effective use of visual history and more accurately distinguishes execution states. Together, these results show that ACE-Brain-0.7 effectively combines spatial perception with temporal understanding, delivering strong execution-grounded reasoning and comparing favorably with closed-source models.

papers.title: Informative Local Average Treatment Effects Using Propensity Scores
papers.authors: Martin Huber, Ying-Ying Lee
papers.what: [Explore] In instrumental variable (IV) models, comparisons of conditional local average treatment effects across covariates can mix effect heterogeneity in observed covariates with changes in the complier population, that is, those whose treatment responds to the instrument. Compliers at
papers.summary: In instrumental variable (IV) models, comparisons of conditional local average treatment effects across covariates can mix effect heterogeneity in observed covariates with changes in the complier population, that is, those whose treatment responds to the instrument. Compliers at different covariate values may differ in unobserved characteristics that may also drive effect heterogeneity. We propose informative conditional local average treatment effects (ICLATEs), which condition on a subset of covariates of interest and on the treatment propensity scores under both values of a binary instrument. Fixing these scores holds constant the range of unobservables that drive treatment selection and thus compliance, while the composition of the covariates not conditioned on may change. Under conditional IV assumptions and suitable support conditions, we establish nonparametric identification and characterize the relationship of the ICLATEs to marginal treatment effects. We distinguish effect homogeneity in the unobservables driving treatment selection from effect homogeneity across excluded covariates. We clarify their roles in extrapolating complier effects to population effects and show that, jointly, they yield a testable implication even with a single binary instrument. For estimation, we combine cross-fitted machine learning of the nuisance functions with pooled local linear regression of doubly robust scores. Under undersmoothing and regularity conditions, we establish pointwise asymptotic normality, which a simulation study supports. As an empirical illustration, we apply the method to the Job Corps program to assess how the earnings effects of training participation vary with age.

papers.title: Network-Adaptive Instrumental Variables
papers.authors: Yi Niu, Zhengyan Xu
papers.what: [Explore] Three mechanisms generate endogeneity in regressions under interference. We address them by constructing network-adaptive instrumental variables (NIV) for a spatial autoregressive (SAR) model with endogenous covariates and unknown network weights. Under network-conditional exclus
papers.summary: Three mechanisms generate endogeneity in regressions under interference. We address them by constructing network-adaptive instrumental variables (NIV) for a spatial autoregressive (SAR) model with endogenous covariates and unknown network weights. Under network-conditional exclusion and information equivalence, the resulting instruments yield valid moments without knowing the true network. We establish joint identification of the structural mean coefficients and the network parameters, providing two sufficient routes. Then under additional covariance restrictions, we identify the disturbance spillover coefficient and the innovation variance. We develop NIV-GMM estimation, establish consistency and asymptotic normality, and give feasible inference and a test for mean network spillovers. Monte Carlo simulations examine their finite-sample performance.

papers.title: Stability Bands for Feature Attribution: The Core, the Nucleolus and the Bargaining Set of Explained-Variance Games
papers.authors: Fernando Delbianco, Fernando Tohmé
papers.what: [Explore] Shapley-value attributions are the default way of explaining machine-learning predictions in economics, but they report a single number per feature and say nothing about whether a coalition of features that jointly accounts for more than it receives could contest that allocation.
papers.summary: Shapley-value attributions are the default way of explaining machine-learning predictions in economics, but they report a single number per feature and say nothing about whether a coalition of features that jointly accounts for more than it receives could contest that allocation. We study feature attribution through the core, the nucleolus and the bargaining set of an explained-variance game, in which the worth of a set of features is the variance of the model's predictions that those features generate. For every feature we report a stability band (its range of shares over the core, or over the least core when the core is empty), with the nucleolus as distinguished point and a certificate that the allocation admits no justified objection. Three results organise the approach. First, for linear models the game is exactly 2-additive, with pairwise Harsanyi dividends $2β_iβ_jσ_{ij}$, so multicollinearity is what creates coalitional structure. Second, in every 2-additive game the prenucleolus coincides with the Shapley value, the (least) core is point-symmetric around it, and the core is non-empty if and only if every cut of the interaction graph has non-negative weight. The Shapley value thus always lies in the prebargaining set, and stability adds information only through band widths and interactions of order three or more. Third, for convex games the bands have a closed form and any allocation can be certified with one minimum cut. In a hedonic price model, the usual mean-SHAP explanation admits a justified objection by the coalition {Ratings, ROM, Battery}. In a gradient-boosting forecaster of retail orders the exact game has an empty core and strong higher-order interactions; the nucleolus departs from the Shapley value by up to 0.19 variance shares, and sparse third-order surrogates recover it where pairwise ones cannot.
